title: Do Deterministic Verifiers Reduce Unsafe LLM‑Generated Network Changes? A Paired Shared‑Candidate Evaluation
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired confirmatory experiment (autocand_A1_prereg_v1) that measured whether coupling a deterministic NetOps verifier+gate (generate→validate→repair, max 1 automated repair) to a single LLM (gpt‑5‑mini) changes safety outcomes when the identical initial LLM candidate is observed with and without gating under shared_initial_candidate semantics. Using 200 deterministically selected paired intents and a sandboxed Batfish‑style validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5), every shared initial candidate passed validation in both baseline and guarded arms (contingency n11=200, n10=0, n01=0, n00=0). The preregistered paired estimand (guarded minus baseline unsafe‑proposal rate) = 0.0; exact two‑sided p = 1.0; 95% paired‑bootstrap percentile CI = [0.0,0.0] (bootstrap_seed=1729, resamples=10000). No automated repairs were applied. Under shared_initial_candidate semantics the confirmatory contrast tests only validator/repair/gate effects on identical first‑pass candidates and does not measure effects from guarded‑conditioned regeneration or multiple independent model samples. We report the preregistered design, artifact‑grounded execution accounting and analysis, interpret the degenerate null in light of ceiling effects, and give artifact‑supported recommendations for follow‑up preregistered designs that avoid degeneracy.

sections.introduction:
Generative language models are increasingly proposed to translate operator intent into concrete device configurations and multi‑step maintenance workflows. Practical adoption requires evidence that LLM‑produced changes will not introduce reachability, isolation, or policy violations when applied to networks. Prior surveys and empirical reports emphasize that operational trustworthiness typically depends on surrounding system machinery—retrieval, deterministic validators, gates, and repair loops—rather than the model alone [1]–[3]. Architectures combining generation with external deterministic validators and bounded repair (generate→validate→repair) are widely advocated in the literature as a practical mitigation path, but reproducible paired evidence that isolates the validator/gate effect on identical model candidates is limited [3],[4].

Research question. For an intent→configuration task bank and a single LLM, does coupling a deterministic validator and a deterministic accept/reject gate (with at most one automated repair attempt) to the identical sampled initial candidate reduce the incidence of unsafe proposals relative to observing that same candidate without gating? We formalized this as the preregistered estimand paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline under shared_initial_candidate semantics.

Contributions. (1) A fully preregistered paired design and frozen execution (autocand_A1_prereg_v1) that fixed generation semantics, sampling, model, validator, gating policy, and analysis prior to observation; (2) an autonomous confirmatory run using gpt‑5‑mini and a Batfish‑style deterministic validator on n=200 deterministically selected paired intents with shared_initial_candidate semantics; (3) artifact‑grounded analysis showing complete concordance (all candidates valid) and no repair activity; (4) an evidence‑rooted interpretation of why the paired contrast is degenerate (ceiling effects) in this run; and (5) concrete artifact‑supported recommendations for follow‑ups designed to produce nondegenerate inference of verifier/gate value.
sections.related_work:
Recent work on LLMs for NetOps and AIOps covers intent‑based configuration translation, runbook generation, RCA, and early agentic automation proposals; surveys emphasize hallucination and unsafe command risks and therefore recommend external checks, RAG anchoring, and validator‑coupled pipelines [1],[2],[5]. In adjacent domains, generate–validate–repair patterns have been empirically explored and, under specific datasets and validators, shown beneficial effects: for example, LLM‑based program‑repair agents and DevOps copilots have demonstrated improved repair rates or safer command suggestions in controlled evaluations [6],[3]. Those adjacent‑domain results motivate validator‑coupled NetOps experiments, but their datasets, validators, and operational constraints differ from network change execution; hence cross‑domain transfer requires careful domain adaptation.

Methodological gaps motivating our design. Two gaps guided our paired protocol. First, comparisons that draw independent first‑pass generations per arm confound validator effects with model sampling variance. Second, many benchmarks target QA/relevance or log/RCA metrics and lack tightly coupled intent→configuration items evaluated under deterministic validators with paired protocols that preserve initial candidate sampling. Our shared_initial_candidate design isolates validator/gate effects on identical initial generations and thus directly addresses the first gap while highlighting how generation semantics condition statistical interpretation.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and frozen plan. We preregistered the study as autocand_A1_prereg_v1. The preregistration fixed: the primary estimand (paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline); generation semantics = shared_initial_candidate; model/adaptor (gpt‑5‑mini via hosted_netops_gvr_v1); deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) and gate policy; repair budget (maximum_repair_calls_per_task = 1); task selection rule and sample size (task_count = 200 paired intents); and the confirmatory analysis executor (paired_binary_analysis_v1). These items and parameter values were frozen before observing outputs and are archived in the execution manifest.

Generation semantics and model sampling clarification (preregistered and executed). The executed and preregistered generation semantics were shared_initial_candidate: exactly one initial LLM generation was produced and deterministically reused for both baseline and guarded arms per paired intent. The run used temperature = null (as recorded in execution/model_configuration.json); null/unset temperature is not evidence of deterministic model sampling (it does not imply temperature = 0). The adapter produced exactly one sampled generation per pair that was deterministically reused for both baseline and guarded arms; we therefore make no claim of deterministic model sampling beyond the single sampled draw per pair. This sentence is included to clarify sampling semantics in the Methods as required by the review.

Models, adapter, validator, and configuration. Declared model: gpt‑5‑mini (execution/model_configuration.json records declared_model_version = "gpt-5-mini" and provider = "openai_responses"). Adapter: hosted_netops_gvr_v1. Deterministic validator: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 implementing Batfish‑style checks (sequence ordering, interface precondition checks, final_group and minimum_up constraints, protected interfaces, and reachability/policy consistency). Model configuration recorded: max_output_tokens=2000, maximum_attempts_per_call=1, reasoning_effort="minimal".

Task bank and deterministic sampling. The deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5 produced intent→configuration items with explicit constraints (allowed_fields, allowed_touched_fields, preserve_unspecified_state, workflow_policies) and required_sequence entries. Sampling followed the adapter's deterministic index rule to select 200 paired intents; selection is fixed and outcome‑independent. The archived task manifest contains per‑task difficulty labels (majority labeled "very_hard" and a minority labeled "extreme").

Interventions, gating, and scoring. Baseline: inspect the shared initial candidate (no validator gating). Guarded: feed the identical shared initial candidate to deterministic_netops_validator_v5; the deterministic gate followed a preregistered accept/reject rule and, upon violations, allowed up to one automated repair attempt (maximum_repair_calls_per_task = 1). Primary outcome: binary unsafe_flag = any reachability or workflow/policy violation reported by the validator after stabilization; scoring used full_intent_constraint_validation and returned score_reason_code values such as VALID_CONFIGURATION.

Confirmatory analysis (frozen). The primary confirmatory analysis used paired_binary_analysis_v1. The 2×2 paired contingency compares unsafe_flag between baseline and guarded across pairs; the analysis reports discordant pair counts (n10, n01), an exact two‑sided McNemar‑equivalent p‑value, and a paired‑bootstrap percentile 95% CI (bootstrap_seed=1729, resamples=10,000). Missingness policy (complete_pair_primary) and a one‑retry rule for infrastructure errors were preregistered.
sections.results:
Execution accounting. The run executed as preregistered (execution manifest): started 2026‑08‑31T13:49:34Z and completed 2026‑08‑31T14:14:32Z. Planned_episode_count = 400; completed_episode_count = 400; failed_episode_count = 0. Model_calls_used = 200 (one shared initial generation per pair). Provider audit recorded hosted_model_call_event_count = 200 and completed_hosted_model_call_event_count = 200.

Primary confirmatory outcome (artifact‑grounded). The paired contingency (guarded × baseline) is n11=200, n10=0, n01=0, n00=0 (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv). Thus every shared initial candidate was scored VALID_CONFIGURATION by deterministic_netops_validator_v5 in both arms. The paired estimate (guarded minus baseline unsafe‑proposal rate) = 0.0; exact two‑sided test p = 1.0. The paired‑bootstrap percentile 95% CI is [0.0,0.0] using bootstrap_seed = 1729 and 10,000 resamples. The zero‑width CI is a direct consequence of no discordant pairs under the registered estimand.

Repair activity and validator diagnostics. repair_applied = false for every guarded episode; repair_provider_trace_path fields are null in the scoring artifacts. Representative episodes show parsed_command_count == required_command_count and violation_count = 0 (e.g., task‑000004 parsed_command_count = 4, required_command_count = 4; validation_after.valid = true). Missingness_summary shows complete_pairs = 200 and zero failed or unscorable episodes.

Latency and operational notes. Because shared_initial_candidate semantics used a single model call per pair, model_call accounting equals 200. The guarded pipeline added deterministic validator time but no repair cycles. Timing logs archived in the execution manifest show validator evaluation dominated the guarded pipeline overhead; exact latency distributions are archived for reproducibility.

Reproducibility. All per‑episode responses, provider traces, validator traces, and analysis artifacts were recorded and archived. Deterministic reconciliation asserts consistent episode accounting and provider call audits; analysis artifacts (condition summary, paired contingency table) reproduce the reported numbers.
sections.discussion:
Artifact‑grounded interpretation of the degenerate null. Under shared_initial_candidate semantics the confirmatory estimand isolates only validator/repair/gate effects on identical first‑pass candidates. Observing n11 = 200 implies that, for the selected model (gpt‑5‑mini), the synthetic task bank, the prompt/template family used, and the deterministic validator's ruleset, the sampled initial candidates already satisfied validator constraints; therefore the guarded machinery applied no repairs and changed no acceptance decisions. The archived artifacts (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv and execution/scoring/*.json) support this conclusion.

Why the paired bootstrap CI is zero‑width. With no discordant pairs every bootstrap resample of paired outcomes yields the same paired difference (0.0), producing zero empirical variance and thus a CI [0.0,0.0]. This is an inferentially valid but degenerate outcome under the chosen estimand and sampling frame.

Ceiling‑effect contributors supported by artifacts. Three concrete contributors are visible in the archive: (1) task‑bank alignment—the generator produced intents whose required_sequence and workflow_policies closely matched the prompt schema, increasing correct syntactic mappings (manifested in required_command_count equals parsed_command_count for representative items); (2) validator tightness—the deterministic_netops_validator_v5 encoded the sequencing and precondition checks that the generator used when creating references, so correct syntactic outputs passed validation readily; and (3) shared_initial_candidate semantics prevented any guarded‑conditioned regeneration or sampling variance that might have produced discordant outcomes. Each contributor is traceable in archived manifests and scoring traces.

Design recommendations. To produce nondegenerate evidence of verifier/gate value we recommend: (a) augmenting the task bank with adversarial or out‑of‑distribution seeds to raise baseline unsafe rates (the archived generator contains generation_seed fields that can be modified to inject adversarial seeds); (b) executing an alternative confirmatory design with independent generation per condition (two independent model calls per pair) or multiple independent samples per condition to capture model sampling variance; (c) testing multiple model variants or temperature settings to reveal sampling sensitivity; and (d) increasing the automated repair budget or enabling iterative repair loops when initial violations are nontrivial. These recommendations follow directly from the execution artifacts and the paired estimand semantics.

Relation to prior work. Our null result does not contradict prior claims that validators can reduce unsafe outputs in other regimes; adjacent studies in program repair and DevOps contexts report empirical improvements under dataset‑specific validators or repair methods [6],[3]. We emphasize that whether a verifier adds measurable benefit depends on task distribution, generation semantics, validator coverage, and sampling regime.
sections.conclusion: We executed a fully preregistered paired experiment under shared_initial_candidate semantics comparing observation of a single LLM initial candidate to feeding that same candidate through a deterministic validator and bounded automated repair. For the chosen model (gpt‑5‑mini), the synthetic task bank, and the validator ruleset, every sampled initial candidate satisfied the deterministic validator and the guarded pipeline applied no repairs; the paired difference = 0.0 (p = 1.0) with a paired‑bootstrap 95% CI = [0.0,0.0]. This null result is specific to the execution frame (model, task bank, validator, and shared_initial_candidate semantics) and therefore does not imply that deterministic validators lack value in realistic or adversarial regimes. We archive full execution and analysis artifacts and recommend follow‑up preregistered designs that increase baseline unsafe rates or permit independent per‑condition generation to quantify verifier/gate contributions under more challenging sampling regimes.

limitations: Internal validity: shared_initial_candidate semantics mean baseline and guarded conditions began from an identical sampled candidate; the confirmatory estimand therefore measures only validator/repair/gate effects on that candidate and cannot assess effects of guarded‑conditioned regeneration or prompt engineering.

Construct validity: tasks were synthetic and deterministically selected; the binary unsafe_flag depends on validator coverage (reachability and workflow sequencing rules) and may not capture all operational risks (transient performance regressions or vendor‑specific side effects outside validator rules).

External validity: single LLM (gpt‑5‑mini), single deterministic validator, and synthetic intents limit generalizability to other models, validators, production topologies, or live device interactions.

Conclusion validity: the observed null effect (paired difference = 0) reflects this execution's sampling frame where baseline generation produced only valid candidates; the study was powered to detect approximately a 10 percentage‑point reduction but cannot rule out smaller effects under different sampling or adversarial inputs.
Operational relevance: no live device changes were executed (sandboxed validation only); operational benefits such as reduced triage time or deployment safety were not measured.
Security/contamination: adversarial or poisoning scenarios were not exercised; no retrieval‑augmented generation (RAG) was used, so retrieval‑based poisoning vectors were not evaluated.

Task‑bank reporting: the archived task_manifest.jsonl is authoritative for per‑label counts; manifest metadata indicates tasks are dominated by 'very_hard' items with a minority labeled 'extreme' (exact per‑label counts are available in the archived manifest).
